title: Spirited Away
full_review:
"Spirited Away" (Disney) is a fantastical, animated adventure about a young Japanese girl named Chihiro who gets lost from her parents and must find her way back to them. Part "Alice in Wonderland" and part "Wizard of Oz," in "Spirited Away" Chihiro (voice of Daveigh Chase) goes through a mysterious tunnel and enters a nightmarish world of spirits and bizarre mythical creatures where she must learn to trust strangers and look within herself to find strength and courage.

The narrative begins in the "real" world as Chihiro and her parents (voiced by Michael Chiklis and Lauren Holly) are driving from their old neighborhood to their new home. From the little interaction between Chihiro and her mother there is a sense that she is a whiny, spoiled child who is terrified of her own shadow.

Like Alice falling down the rabbit hole or Dorothy getting swept up in a tornado, Chihiro is transformed from her reality to an outrageous otherworld where almost anything imagined is possible -- and her name is changed to Sen. It is never quite clear if she is having a nightmare, or if the spirit world is actually taking over as her parents enter a forest that is filled with shrines and pagan symbols of Japanese culture.

As things begin to get weird, her parents enter a seemingly abandoned restaurant that is filled with giant platters of food. They begin to eat until they turn into enormous pigs. Terrified, Chihiro runs into the darkened streets that are now filled with shadowy spirit figures. There she meets a young man named Haku (voice of Jason Marsden) who takes her by the hand and leads her to a castle-like building that is a bathhouse run by the wicked witch Yubaba (voice of Susanne Pleshette).

Ironically, everywhere Chihiro turns she is given mixed signals. It is never immediately clear whether people are trying to help her or hurt her. In this fantastic new world where oversized babies turn into little rats, she is given a series of odd clues that help her to survive and get safely back to her parents and home.

As written and directed by Hayao Miyazaki, the brilliant animation in "Spirited Away" operates on different levels. It shows how the adult world is confusing and harsh to children and how they learn from their experience as well as their own inner strength to get past what they perceive to be scary obstacles in order to get what they want and need. It also shows how it can be a child's nature to trust and their need to follow their own instincts.

Unlike any other Disney film, "Spirited Away" introduces American audiences to new layers of Japanese and Asian culture, including some of its Western influences. After detailed scenes of her grueling bathhouse chores and initiations, Chihiro re-enters the forest and comes upon a cottage that might be found in a "Hansel and Gretel" or "Little Red Riding Hood" story. "Spirited Away" ultimately has a fairytale happy ending as Chihiro makes it through her own personal journey, finding love and friendship.

Filled with serpents, faceless monsters, a giant radish and river spirits, this imaginative Japanese story takes some getting used to and may be too menacing for the very young, although less so for older, pre-teen youngsters.

Due to some frightening images, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested.
